steps.title: Endings tell you what a word can do in a sentence
steps.html:
English builds most of its abstract nouns out of verbs and adjectives, and the ending is the signal. If you know the ending, you know where the word can stand: after the, after no, as a subject, after a preposition. Getting this wrong — no relevant, very proficiency — is one of the most visible errors at this level, because it makes an otherwise accurate sentence unreadable.

From verbs. -ment and -tion / -ation do most of this work. Measure gives measurement, achieve gives achievement, adjust gives adjustment. Observe gives observation, introduce gives introduction, customize gives customization. A small group takes neither: yield, use and increase are their own nouns already.

From adjectives. -ity is the commonest: scarce → scarcity, able → ability, flexible → flexibility, specific → specificity. Adjectives ending in -ant and -ent take -ance and -ence: relevant → relevance, significant → significance, different → difference. A subgroup in -ent and -icient prefers -cy: proficient → proficiency, efficient → efficiency. -ness is the reliable fallback for short, everyday adjectives: aware → awareness, willing → willingness.

Spelling. The final -e is kept before -ment (achievement) and dropped before -ity and -ation (scarcity, observation). Adjectives in -y change to -i before -ness: happy → happiness.

steps.title: Where each form can stand
steps.html:
• noun: after the, a, no, some, or a preposition — the relevance of…, no measurement, with great difficulty
  • adjective: after be, seem, very, or before a noun — very proficient, a specific reason
  • verb: after a subject — most people overestimate…
  • A quick test: if very fits in front of it, it is an adjective; if the fits, it is a noun.

steps.title: Text A · Why the eyes are not the problem
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Rayner et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest 17(1), 2016, and Brysbaert’s meta-analysis of adult reading rates.

Most adults read far more slowly than they believe they do. A review of 190 studies covering more than eighteen thousand participants put the average silent reading rate for adults in English at around 238 words a minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction. Ask people to estimate their own rate and they overestimate it, sometimes by a factor of two. The gap between what people do and what they think they do is the first thing any honest discussion of speed has to deal with. Careful measurement of reading speed is old and well established, which is part of what makes the claims of the speed-reading industry so easy to test.

The real limit is not the eyes. It is tempting to assume that a proficient reader is simply one whose eyes move efficiently, but the movement of the eyes accounts for no more than about a tenth of the total time spent reading. The rest goes on recognising each word and working out how the words combine. That is a language problem, not an optical one, and no training can make it disappear.

Speed-reading programmes generally work by removing something that turns out to be useful. The industry is not new — Evelyn Wood launched her training programme in 1959 — but it now includes a multitude of apps that flash single words on a screen so that the reader cannot look back. Looking back is exactly the problem. Skilled readers constantly make reference to words they have already passed, and most of those backward movements exist to repair a misunderstanding. Prevent them and the misunderstanding simply stays where it is.

steps.title: Text B · What is left, once the promises are removed
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Rayner et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest 17(1), 2016.

The evidence on trained speed readers points consistently in one direction. Studies of people who have completed such courses find that the increase in speed comes with a reduction in comprehension; the achievement is real, but it is not the achievement advertised. Investigations of the most impressive performers usually reveal something simpler: they already knew a great deal about the subject. Without that prior knowledge, the same readers cannot answer substantive questions about what they have supposedly read.

Skimming, however, is a genuine skill and a defensible one. If a full understanding is not the goal, a reader can move through a text much faster and come away with moderate comprehension — enough to judge relevance, locate specific information, and decide whether the piece deserves a proper reading. Skimmers do this by reading headings, first sentences and key words, which is why the significance of a well-built paragraph is practical rather than decorative. Given the scarcity of attention most readers are working with, a paragraph that announces its own subject in its first line lets them get on with the argument instead of hunting for it.

The only reliable route to reading faster is unglamorous. The more often a reader has met a word, the more quickly it is processed, so wider reading and a larger vocabulary yield modest but genuine and measurable gains over time. This is slower than any course promises, which is presumably why people drop out of the courses and give up on the apps. It amounts to advice nobody wants: read more, look words up, and do your best with a text before deciding it is too hard.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
The goal I have failed at three times was never specific enough to start. “Get better at Portuguese” is not a plan; it is a wish with a language attached. Each January I set it, and each February I gave up, because nothing in it told me what to do on a particular Tuesday evening.

The version that survives has a measurement in it. Thirty minutes, four mornings a week, and one page of written notes at the end of each session. That is small enough to be dull and specific enough to be checked. By the third week the notes themselves are the evidence: either there are twelve pages or there are not.

The plan is built around the hours that exist rather than the ones I would like. An honest reference of my week yields about three free hours, not eight, and the scarcity is the useful part. Two of those hours are already spoken for by the mornings, which leaves one for the week when everything goes wrong.

What would end it is not difficulty but silence. If, after two months, nothing measurable has changed, I will stop and say so rather than let it fade. The relevance of this plan is not that it is ambitious; it is that the achievement it asks for is one I could reach without any change to my life at all.
